newsitem.title: USA: Floods hurt US spring wheat acres, prices entice.
newsitem.headline: Floods hurt US spring wheat acres, prices entice.

text.p: The recent rise in U.S. wheat prices may spark an increase in spring wheat plantings in North Dakota and Minnesota, helping to compensate for acres lost to flooding in the Red River Valley, agronomists said.

"There will be more inticement to plant a little more wheat," said North Dakota State University agronomist Kent McKay, noting much of the expected switching from spring wheat to soybeans this year had been price based.
New crop spring wheat prices on the Minneapolis Grain Exchange have risen around 50 cents a bushel since late March.
During that period, new crop soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade have dropped about 25 cents.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's March planting survey forecast a cut in North Dakota's hard red spring wheat acreage of 20 percent to 7.7 million acres. Soybean acres in the state were seen rising 35 percent to 1.1 million.

University of Minnesota agronomist Lee Hardman, said floods would delay planting in the Red River Valley, leading to some shifting in the southern part of the area from other crops to soybeans. Most farmers would, however, probably try for as long as possible to stick with their original plans.

"They are probably still going to plant wheat (despite yield penalties) because it is wheat they are ready for," Hardman said, also noting those holding crop insurance needed to plant the planned crop to receive payments.
He noted that the region's sugarbeet crop could be the most severely hurt by the current floods.

"The big penalty crop (in terms of yield loss for late planting) is sugarbeet. They (farmers) won't want to switch though, as it is a big return crop and in some cases they are locked into a rotation," Hardman said.
Figures issued by the North Dakota Agricultural Statistics Service show in 1996 about 94 percent of the state's 226,600 sugar beet acres were in counties bordering the Red River.
In neighboring Minnesota a slightly lower 71 percent of the state's 441,000 sugar beet acres in 1996 were planted in counties bordering the Red River, government statistics show.
"Sugarbeet and small grains are the two main crops which are going to take a hit," Hardman said.
Lance Gaebe, executive director of the North Dakota Grain Growers Association, said wheat acres would be lost in the Red River Valley and late planting could hurt the state's yields.
"It's cold and wet, nothing is going on. We are going to have late planting right across the whole state," he said.
Gaebe said acres would be lost both in the flooded area and in other parts of the state.
"Those closest to the flooded areas may not be able to plant at all because it is going to be extraordinarily wet," he said noting in other areas wetlands were likely to be much larger than normal.
"Where you might normally have an acre (under water), you have got three acres this year," he said.
Government statistics show that 58 percent (1.49 million acres) of the 2.55 million acres of spring wheat planted in Minnesota last year were in areas bordering the Red River.
The USDA's March survey put Minnesota spring wheat plantings this year down just 50,000 acres at 2.5 million.
In North Dakota 1.79 million acres were planted to spring wheat last year in counties bordering the river, representing 19 percent of the state's 9.6 million acre plantings.
